result.summary: The gods decide Ulysses must leave Calypso, and Mercury delivers Jove's order. Ulysses builds a raft and sails, but Neptune wrecks it. Helped by Ino and Minerva, he reaches Phaeacian land and sleeps under two olive shoots.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Minerva pleads for Ulysses and Jove orders Mercury to tell Calypso to release him.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is stranded and suffering, and Telemachus is threatened by the suitors.

scenes.title: Mercury visits Calypso
scenes.summary: Mercury delivers Jove's decree. Calypso protests but yields, and then looks for Ulysses on the shore.
scenes.stakes: Calypso risks Jove's anger if she refuses, and loses Ulysses if she obeys.

scenes.title: Building the raft
scenes.summary: Calypso swears an oath and helps Ulysses build a raft. He sails for seventeen days and sights Phaeacia.
scenes.stakes: A dangerous sea voyage on a raft.

scenes.title: Neptune's storm
scenes.summary: Neptune raises a storm and wrecks the raft. Ino gives Ulysses her veil, and Minerva calms the winds so he drifts toward land.

scenes.title: Landing and sleep
scenes.summary: Ulysses is battered by the surf and prays to a river god. He lands and sleeps in a leaf bed under the olives.
scenes.stakes: Exhaustion, cold and wild beasts could kill him.

Ulysses prefers mortal Penelope to an immortal goddess.

analysis.text: Ulysses chooses mortal life and home over immortality, and his endurance is tested again by Neptune's wrath.
Calypso's complaint shows the gods punishing unions between goddesses and mortal men, a pattern in Greek myth.

legacy.text: The name Calypso gave its name to the calypso musical style, and Jacques Cousteau's ship Calypso was named after her.

fun_facts.text: Ulysses is the Latin name for Odysseus; this translation (Samuel Butler's) uses Roman names for the gods.

language_notes.text: Dawn's couch beside Tithonus refers to the goddess Aurora (Dawn), whose mortal husband Tithonus was Trojan; a stock formula for daybreak.
Minerva's wish is ironic and bitter: she hopes no ruler will be kind, to shame the gods into acting for Ulysses.
"Hurry-skurrying" is a playful, colloquial rendering describing the suitors scrambling back in failure.
"Convoyed" means escorted; Ulysses will travel without divine or human company.
"Slayer of Argus" recalls Mercury killing the hundred-eyed giant Argus, who guarded Io for Juno.
Pieria is a region in northern Greece, near Mount Olympus, which Mercury crosses on his flight.
Warp means the lengthwise threads on a loom; the shuttle carries the weft thread across them.
Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods, thought to confer immortality.
Hecatombs were large sacrifices of cattle, originally a hundred, offered to the gods.
"Most ill-starred" means most unlucky, as if born under a bad star; it refers to Ulysses.
Dawn loved the hunter Orion; the gods resented it, and Diana (the Greek Artemis) killed him on Ortygia, an island.
Ceres (the Greek Demeter) lay with Iasion in a field ploughed three times; Jove struck him dead with a thunderbolt.
"My poor fellow" is a sympathetic address; Calypso speaks with warmth and condescension, pitying his grief.
Swearing by the river Styx was the gods' most binding oath; even Olympian gods could not break it without severe penalty.
Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods, conferring immortality, in contrast to mortal meat and drink.
A girdle is a belt or sash worn around the waist; gossamer means very fine, light cloth.
An adze is a cutting tool with an arched blade set at right angles to the handle, used to shape timber.
Augers are tools for boring holes in wood.
Sailors steered by the Pleiads, Bootes and the Bear (Big Dipper). Keeping the Bear on the left means sailing eastward.
"Days seven and ten" is an inverted way of saying seventeen days.
The Ethiopians were a distant people at the edge of the world, whom Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) was fond of visiting to receive sacrifices.
Danaans, like Achaeans, is a Homeric name for the Greeks. 'Thrice blest' is an old intensifying phrase.
Refers to the fight over Achilles' corpse at Troy, when Ulysses held off the Trojans while Ajax carried the body away.
Battledore and shuttlecock is an old game, like badminton, in which a shuttlecock is batted back and forth.
Aegae was Neptune's underwater palace home, where he kept his horses.
'Bound the ways of all the winds' means she held them back, confining them; only the North wind was left blowing.
"Some angry spirit" means a hostile divinity (daimon) thought to cause illness; the simile pictures a sick father's recovery.
Amphitrite is Neptune's wife, queen of the sea, and mother of sea creatures; hence the monsters she "breeds".
A polypus is an octopus; its suckers grip the rock as Ulysses grips the stones.
A spit that "takes the waves aslant" is a point of land where waves strike at an angle and do less harm.
"Cling to the knees" is the ritual gesture of a suppliant begging protection; here it is applied figuratively to the river god.
Ino, the sea goddess, earlier gave Ulysses the scarf (veil) that kept him afloat; he returns it as she instructed.
A sucker is a shoot growing from a root; one olive is wild (ungrafted), the other cultivated (grafted), sharing a stock.
"Brand" means a burning log or ember; "fire-seed" is the preserved spark from which a fire can be restarted.

context_notes.text: Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and wields the thunderbolt.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours Ulysses; Calypso is a nymph who has kept him on her island for years.
Telemachus went to Pylos and Lacedaemon to ask Nestor and Menelaus for news of his father.
Mercury is the gods' messenger, often sent to carry commands between realms.
The Phaeacians of Scheria are a seafaring people, kin to the gods, who will give Ulysses passage home.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is Jove's messenger god, known for winged sandals and his sleep-giving wand.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) was angered because the Greeks failed to punish the outrage against her temple at Troy.
Calypso offered Ulysses immortality and eternal youth if he stayed with her as husband.
Mercury had just visited Calypso with Jove's command to release Ulysses, who had been held on her island, Ogygia, for years.
Calypso offers immortality, which Ulysses will refuse in favour of returning to his mortal wife.
The Phaeacians are the seafaring people of Scheria, who will eventually take Ulysses home to Ithaca.
The trident is Neptune's emblem; as god of the sea he can stir up storms and winds with it.
Ino was a mortal princess of Thebes who became the sea goddess Leucothea, a protector of sailors.
The veil is a divine talisman that keeps Ulysses afloat and safe; returning it to the sea is a ritual of gratitude.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is angry because Ulysses blinded his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' protector among the gods, and often helps him with timely thought.
Ulysses does not know the river's name, so he addresses the god politely as "whoever you may be," a common ancient practice.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses' rule is compared to a father's, stressing his kindness and the ingratitude of those who forgot him.
Jove's gentle teasing, "my dear," shows an indulgent father and reveals that Minerva already planned Ulysses' return.
Jove's summary closes the decision plainly, settling the plot's direction and giving the gods' authority over fate.
Mercury's low flight over the waves is compared to a cormorant fishing, making the god's movement vivid and bird-like.
The lush vine, running streams and violets create an idyllic, paradise-like setting that makes Ulysses' longing to leave more poignant.
Calypso's angry outburst shows her passion and sense of injustice, yet she is quickly forced to submit to Jove.
Ulysses lives with a goddess in a paradise yet is miserable, his captor's love contrasting with his grief.
Ulysses suspects a trick, but the reader knows the gods have ordered his release, so Calypso's offer is sincere.
A heart "made of iron" expresses harshness; Calypso claims to be tender and sympathetic.
"Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a recurring Homeric formula marking the start of a new day.
The distant mountains rising "like a shield" convey their rounded, dark shape on the horizon, and hint at safety.
Ulysses' lament envies the dead heroes, showing his despair and his longing for a glorious death over a pitiful one.
The tossed raft is compared to thistledown whirled along a road, stressing how light and helpless it is against the wind.
Ino rises like a sea-gull, linking the goddess to the sea birds and marking her sudden, gentle appearance.
The raft breaking apart like dry chaff in a whirlwind conveys how fragile it is against Neptune's wrath.
Neptune grimly says Ulysses will not find he was let off lightly, though Ulysses will in fact reach safety at last.
Ulysses' relief at seeing land is compared to children's joy at a father's recovery, giving his gratitude emotional warmth.
The octopus torn from its bed, stones clinging, extends the comparison to show how violently the rocks strip the skin from his hands.
Ulysses debates his options aloud to himself, revealing his anxiety and careful reasoning at a moment of exhaustion.
Ulysses buried in leaves is likened to a hidden ember in ashes, suggesting life preserved and kept safe until it can rekindle.
